senses.gloss:
kaivalya
(‘being all alone’)
------------------------------------------
Liberation from the seemingly endless cycle of birth and death has been posited by all the six systems of Hindu philosophy, as the final goal of life. This goal has been variously described as: मुक्ति, मोक्ष, कैवल्य and निर्वाण.
Kaivalya is a technical word used mostly by the Sāṅkhya and योग philosophies. Literally it means ‘kevalatva’ or ‘being all alone’. The पुरुष or the individual सोउल् who was in bondage due to his association and identification with प्रधान or प्रकृति (insentient nature, matrix of material च्रेअतिओन्) realises by the practice of योग that he is absolutely different and separate from it. This know-ledge—called ‘vivekakhyāti’—frees him from that bondage and so becomes himself once again and ‘all alone’, never again under the स्लवेर्य् of प्रकृति (vide Yogasūtras 4.34).

Kaivalya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad classed among the Śaiva उपनिषद्स् and assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. There are 25 mantras, mostly in the śloka metre.
The sage आश्वलायन approaches ब्रह्मा (creator)—called Parameṣṭhi here—and requests him to teach ब्रह्मविद्या (knowledge of ब्रह्मन्) so that he can destroy all the sins and attain the highest पुरुष or God.
After advising the disciple to cultivate faith and devotion to know the Truth, ब्रह्मा declares that this knowledge can be attained by त्याग or renunciation alone and not by rituals or progeny or wealth. Those who have obtained the knowledge of Vedānta, who have purified themselves through saṁnyāsayoga or the spirit of renunciation, they go to ब्रह्मलोक and attain final लिबेरतिओन् at the end of the cycle of च्रेअतिओन् when even the ब्रह्मलोक gets dissolved in the Supreme ब्रह्मन्.
In order to get this, the aspirant has to meditate on Lord शिव, along with his divine consort Umā (Pārvatī), in the lotus of the heart, after sitting in a suitable posture in a lonely and pure place conducive to the practice of योग.
When this meditation ripens into समाधि, he realises his identity with the Lord. He becomes one with ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव as also इन्द्र, प्राण (vital airs), kāla (time) and so on. Having thus become one with everything, past, present and future, he transcends death.
The teacher then describes the process of meditation on the Self inside by giving the analogy of the araṇis (See ARAṆIS.) which are used to generate fire for वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
The topic discussed next is that of the जीव (the individual सोउल्). In reality he is the Supreme सोउल् (Paramātman) from whom the whole universe evolves, but now apparently in bondage due to the effect of māyā (creative, illusory power of the Lord). Due to this apparent bondage only, he experiences the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (waking, dream and deep-sleep).
Brahmā then teaches आश्वलायन that the जीव (individual सोउल्) in essence is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, is the witness of all the three states and is ब्रह्मन् itself in reality. It is this realisation of identity that frees him from all bondage.
The last part of the Upaniṣad describes the subjective experience of a realised सोउल्. He is smaller than the smallest, bigger than the biggest, without limbs and parts, can get all knowledge without the aid of the senses, and, in reality is शिव himself.
The Upaniṣad concludes with an advice to the unenlightened, to repeat the Śatarudriya (Rudrādhyāya) in order to get enough purity of मिन्द्, ultimately leading to कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन्.
See also UPANIṢADS.
